sentences.text: There is a post at the end of the inner wall at Porthallow that used to hold a light and has held nothing since 1988, and a cormorant sits on it.
The light was taken off when the new one went on the outer arm and the post was left because taking a post out of a Cornish harbour wall is a great deal more work than leaving it in.
It is oak, about two metres proud, black, with four iron bolts in it that have wept rust down the stone for forty years.
Cormorants sit on posts.
It is what they are for, more or less.

They have wettable feathers, which is the trade they have made in exchange for being able to chase a fish underwater at a depth that would kill most birds, and it means that after a session in the water they have to get out and stand somewhere with their wings open like a wet umbrella until they are dry.
Every harbour in Britain has one on a post and nobody looks at it twice.
Merryn has since spent a career explaining to people that this is not a design fault.

A bird that could stay dry would float too well, and a bird that floats too well cannot get down to forty metres and stay there for a minute, and the cormorant has traded comfort for a hunting depth that no other British seabird of its size gets anywhere near.
The wet umbrella on the post is not a bird recovering from a mistake.
It is the running cost of being extremely good at something.

What Merryn's family will tell you about the one at Porthallow — and what her grandmother will tell you at length, and what her uncle will tell you shortly and while looking at something else — is that she is on that post at the start of the ebb, when the boats go, and she is on it when they come back.
And in between, if they are all in, she goes.
If they are not all in, she does not.
Nobody in Porthallow claims she is counting.
Merryn wants that on the record because it is the version that gets repeated by visitors and it is not what anybody there actually says.
What her grandmother said, always in the same words, was: *she's not off yet.* Merryn tested this properly at twelve because she had reached the age at which you test what your family tells you.

She did it for the whole of a summer with a notebook and a pair of binoculars from her bedroom window, which looks down the harbour, and the method was simple: count the boats out, count the boats in, and record whether the post was occupied at three-hourly intervals.
She was rigorous about the parts she could be rigorous about, which is a thing she is still proud of.
She wrote the boat count before she looked at the post, every time, so that she could not adjust one to fit the other.
She had a rule that a bird had to be on the post at the moment she looked and not within a minute of it.
She had no rule at all about how hard she looked, which is where the whole thing falls apart, and it took her until about nineteen to see it.
Fifty-eight days.
Eleven days on which every boat was back within the usual window and the post was empty by an hour after.
Forty-four days on which she could not get a clean count because of visitors, weather or her own laziness.
The forty-four is the honest number and it is the one she puts in first now.

Doing anything properly for fifty-eight consecutive days at twelve turned out to be about four times harder than she had estimated, and the reason she remembers that summer at all is mostly that she failed at it.
And three days on which a boat was late, and on all three of those the post had a cormorant on it, and on two of the three that cormorant was still there in the dark.
The third one came in at half past four in the afternoon with a broken hydraulic and the post was empty by six.
